nameStory: The retrovert pteropod gets its name from its backwards-turning shell - 'retrovert' means turned backward or reversed. The common name 'sea butterfly' comes from the way these tiny creatures gracefully 'fly' through the water using wing-like extensions of their body, fluttering through the ocean like butterflies through air.
description: The retrovert pteropod is a tiny swimming sea snail that looks like a cross between a snail and a butterfly. These translucent creatures have delicate, coiled shells that spiral backwards and slug-like bodies with wing-like flaps they use to 'fly' through the water. They're part of a group called sea butterflies, and despite being snails, they spend their entire lives floating in the open ocean rather than crawling on the bottom.

idTips.label: Backwards-coiled shell
idTips.description: The thin, translucent shell coils in the opposite direction from most snails, creating a distinctive left-handed spiral that feels delicate and papery to the touch

idTips.label: Wing-like swimming appendages
idTips.description: Two transparent, fluttering extensions from the body that beat rhythmically like tiny wings, propelling the animal through the water with graceful undulations

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: The soft body appears glassy and see-through, often with a slight iridescent shimmer that catches light as it moves through the water

idTips.label: Planktonic swimming behavior
idTips.description: Unlike bottom-dwelling snails, these creatures are always found floating freely in the water column, never crawling on surfaces

habitat: Retrovert pteropods live in the open waters off New England's coast, particularly in the cold surface waters of the Gulf of Maine and Georges Bank. You'll only encounter them in the ocean itself - never in bays, estuaries, or nearshore areas. They prefer the cooler waters found in deeper offshore areas where cold currents bring nutrient-rich water to the surface.

seasonality.spring: Most likely to be spotted during spring plankton blooms when they may be more abundant in surface waters. Look for them during calm weather when the water is clear.
seasonality.summer: Present in offshore waters but may be deeper during warmer months. Best chance of observation is from research vessels or during whale watching trips in deeper waters.
seasonality.fall: May become more visible again as water temperatures cool and they potentially move closer to the surface in their feeding areas.
seasonality.winter: Present year-round but rarely observable due to rough winter seas making offshore observation difficult for casual naturalists.

funFact: These tiny sea butterflies are actually predators that hunt other floating plankton using a sticky mucus web they cast like an invisible net - despite looking delicate and harmless, they're the wolves of the microscopic ocean world!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small jellyfish or planktonic animals when seen swimming. The key difference is the obvious coiled shell - no other floating creature in New England waters combines wing-like swimming with a snail shell.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sea butterflies,' these are actually true snails - they're gastropods just like garden snails, but have evolved to live their entire lives floating in open water. The term 'pteropod' means 'wing-foot,' referring to how their foot has evolved into wing-like swimming appendages.
compareHints: Since this is the only Limacina species documented in New England waters, compare it to other sea butterflies in the pteropod group. Retrovert pteropods are distinguished by their distinctly backwards-coiled shell, while other sea butterflies may have straight shells or shells that coil in the typical right-handed direction.
